problems.stem: An evidence-collection row reads: "The AI tool improved student writing." What is missing for this to count as evidence?
options: A longer sentence describing the tool.
The artifact, where it is stored, and the date range, so another teacher could locate and inspect it.
A statement that the teacher liked the tool.
problems.explanation: A claim with no cited artifact or source is an opinion. Evidence names what can be located and inspected.

problems.stem: A row claims the AI revision coach raised organization scores. What must the checklist include for that claim to be testable?
options: A note that students seemed happier.
A pre-tool baseline scored on the same rubric, so the before and after can be compared.
The number of students in the class.
The brand name of the tool.
problems.explanation: Improvement implies a before and an after measured the same way. Without a baseline the claim cannot be tested.

problems.stem: A teacher only records the cases where the AI coach seemed to help. What habit makes the evidence stronger?
options: Collecting even more examples that confirm the tool helped.
Stating what would have changed your mind and checking for it, for example whether weaker writers gained less.
Deleting any result that does not fit the conclusion.
Asking the tool whether it helped.
problems.explanation: Strong evidence can be disconfirmed. Looking for the counter-case (who gained less) bounds and strengthens the claim.

problems.stem: Which checklist entry best makes a result verifiable by someone other than the teacher who collected it?
options: The result felt clear to me.
22 paired drafts are stored in the unit folder; a colleague can re-score 5 random pairs blind on the same 4-point rubric.
The class agreed the tool was useful.
I remember the scores going up.
problems.explanation: Stored artifacts plus a stated re-check method let an independent reader confirm the result, which is what makes it evidence.
